1: nox erat: the speaker concisely establishes a nighttime setting. The formula appears elsewhere in Ovid (e.g., Fasti 1.421, 2.792, 3.639, 6.673) but is likely adopted from Vergil (Aeneid 3.147, 4.522, and 8.26). summisit = submisit: “lowered” (OLD s.v. submitto 7)
2: uisa: “dreams” (OLD s.v. uisum). The origin of the form is the perfect passive participle of uidēre. meum: a first-person singular speaker is subtly introduced.
3: The description of the dream setting in this and the next couplet is reminiscent of a locus amoenus. See the Grammar Commentary for Amores 3.1.4 for more on this literary topos. ilice: the ablative specifies in what respect the lucus was creberrimus (A&G 418).
5: area: the final a is short. The consonantal cluster gr- does not consistently make the syllable preceding it long by position. prato: dative with suberat (OLD s.v. subsum 1b and 1c).
6: umida: scansion shows that this adjective modifies area in the previous verse. lene: an adverb modifying sonantis aquae. The water’s source is not specified, but this adverb suggests a stream rather than a rushing river. (For vocabulary describing a rushing river, see Amores 3.6, especially vv. 7-8 and 85-86.)
7: ipse … uitabam: the speaker places himself within the dream. Note the graphic word order, with uitabam surrounded by the tree leaves, the heat seemingly excluded.
8: sed: the postponed conjunction compresses into the verse’s final feet the surprising ineffectiveness of the speaker’s evasive action. The repetition between vv. 7 and 8 highlights the futility of the speaker’s effort to stay out of the heat, perhaps adding a sense of comic exasperation. The “spell” of a locus amoenus (see n. 3) is broken.
9: ecce: the speaker gestures dramatically to the arrival of someone or something, but the nominative subject is postponed to the next verse. immixtas: the synchesis, or interlocking word order, graphically represents how the turf is intermixed with flowers.
10: uacca: the subject of the couplet appears near the end of its second verse. Note the hyperbaton of uacca and its adjective petens in v. 9. The subject is also “surrounded” by the speaker’s eyes (oculos candida uacca meos). Should a first-time reader think this could be a puella? The earliest hint that it is not is that she is seeking not flowers but grass.
11: The speaker compares the heifer’s coloring to snow and fresh milk in this and the following couplet. candidior: see the Grammar Commentary for Amores 3.7.8 for this same word in the context of a maiden’s snow-white skin. cecidere = syncopated form of cediderunt. The subject niues must be supplied from context. recentes: can be smoothly translated as an adverb.
12: quas: the postponement of this relative pronoun to the middle of the verse encourages readers to interpret it separately from in liquidas aquas. The antecedent is niuibus in the previous verse. A rendering of the relative clause in English word order might yield the following: niuibus … quas mora nondum uertit in liquidas aquas. The snow has yet to melt.
13: quod: another occasion of challenging word order. The antecedent lacte is embedded in the middle of the relative clause. (Kenney sets it off with commas to ease reading.) A rendering of the couplet in English word order might yield the following: candidior lacte quod albet adhuc stridentibus spumis et modo reliquit siccatam ouem. The word order in this couplet feels particularly unOvidian. See notes in Davis adhuc: “still.” Since milk is unlikely to become less white with time, this adverb may better modify stridentibus than albet.
15: huic: dative of possession (A&G 373). feliciter: the adverb suggests that the bull feels fortunate to be the heifer’s “husband” rather than the idea that the bull is simply happy (felix). maritus: while comes permits some ambiguity, maritus emphatically identifies the bull as the heifer’s mate (cf. coniuge in v. 16).
16: teneram … pressit humum: the sense is clarified by iacet in the next verse. cumque sua … coniuge: although the bull is with the heifer, the heifer is not lying down; she is described as standing in v. 10.
17: iacet: the narrative follows the bull. reuocatas: a colorful participle to describe the regurgitated cud. Alliteration with r in this verse and with t and p in the next conveys repeated action of (re)chewing.
18: atque iterum pasto pascitur ante cibo: “and again he grazes on previously grazed food.” pasto pascitur: the polyptoton again illustrates the chewing of cud, also emphasized by iterum. This verse doesn’t really convey anything that hasn’t already been conveyed in the previous one, but the repetition is surely the point.
19: The couplet reads more smoothly in English if the ablative absolute phrase is translated last. A rendering in English word order might yield the following: uisus erat deposuisse terra cornigerum caput, somno adimente uires ferendi (id = caput). ferendi: the gerund’s implied object (caput) appears in the next verse.
21: The postponement of the verb to beginning of the next verse emphasizes the crow’s gliding arrival.
22: garrula: Ovid uses the same word for the chattering of a crow in Metamorphoses 2.547.
23: terque: S supplies terque, while manuscripts P and Y read perque. (Y also writes uobis for bouis. See the Manuscript Commentary.) bouis niueae: the narrative pivots to the heifer now that the bull is asleep.
24: fodit: as with the previous couplet, the postponed verb creates enjambment between the two verses. abstulit: with its theft of the tufts of hair, the crow abruptly leaves the dream and the narrative.
25: illa = uacca diu cunctata: might the lengthy delay shift some responsibility to the bull, who sleeps through the entire affair?
26: niger … liuor: the location of the black spot on the heifer’s chest confirms a causal connection to the actions of the crow (pectora, v. 23).
27: Another couplet built around repetition between the hexameter and pentameter (cf. vv. 7-8), but unlike in the prior one, the pentameter verse here provides little additional detail besides the fact that the pabula is laeta. Kenney places the entire verse in parentheses, presenting it as an aside in speaker’s narrative.
29: illuc: the heifer’s departure for green pastures (quite literally; see herbae fertilioris in v. 30) is indicated with spatial adverbs (cf. huc, v. 21).
31: dic age: the first internal indication that the speaker is addressing an interlocutor. Kenney places a quotation mark at the beginning of the poem, but an ancient reader would have no such marking to aid in recognizing the quoted speech. nocturnae … imaginis augur: “interpreter of a nighttime image” = “interpreter of dreams” quicumque es: the speaker does not seem to be familiar with this divinatory addressee.
32: Inverting the two clauses in this verse and placing the interrogative quid first in its clause eases English translation: dic … quid ista uisa ferant, siquid habent ueri. habent: the subject can be resupplied from ista uisa. The object is (ali)quid ueri, with ueri functioning as a partitive genitive (A&G 346).
33: sic ego: the speaker clearly marks the conclusion of his narrated speech.
34: expendens: “weighing.” The speaker feels the interpreter’s words are thoughtfully considered.
35: The next five couplets quote (cf. sic dixit in v. 33) the interpreter’s explanation of various details in the dream. quem: by placing the relative clause first, the interpreter can postpone his interpretation to the end of the verse. uitare: it is unclear why the speaker would want to avoid the heat of love.
37: aptus color ille: the interpreter addresses the speaker’s attention to the heifer’s coloring.
39: quod: “as to the fact that.” A substantive clause with quod and the indicative. This one acts as an accusative of specification (A&G 572a).
40: dominae = the speaker’s puellae lena … anus: an aged procuress or “madame” would control access to the puella, often (as far as the elegist is concerned) out of spite. See the Grammar Note on Amores 3.1.44. mouebit: the interpreter seems to offer the speaker some reason for hope: the actions of the lena are still in the future.
41: quod: “as to the fact that.” See n. 39, above.
42: sua: focalizes the experience of the bull. destituere = destitueris (future passive indicative) uiduo: “bereft of a lover.”
43: liuor et … maculae: the markings left by the crow seem to be proliferating (cf. liuor in v. 26).
44: A rendering of the indirect statement in English word order might yield the following: … negant pectus carere labe adulterii. The present tense negant offers less hope for avoiding the dream’s prediction than the future tense mouebit and destituere in vv. 40 and 42. The “mark of adultery” (adulterii labe) seems already to be present.
45: dixerat: the speaker resumes the narrative, no longer speaking aloud but recounting his reaction to the interpreter’s words. mihi: consider translating this dative of reference (A&G 376) or ethical dative (A&G 377) as a possessive adjective (i.e., meus sanguis).
46: nox: night is imminent. Has the speaker grown pale from what he has just heard … or in anticipation of the dreams the next night may bring?
